lesson.title: How Far Off Can You Be? The Standard Deviation of p-hat
lesson.summary: The standard deviation of the sampling distribution of p-hat is the square root of p times one minus p, divided by n, and it measures how much sample proportions typically vary from the true population proportion.
lesson.body:
Knowing that the sampling distribution of p-hat is centered on p, from the previous chapter, tells you nothing about how spread out that distribution is. Two sampling distributions can share the same mean but look completely different: one tightly clustered around p, another scattered widely around it. The standard deviation of p-hat measures that spread, and it is what lets us judge whether a particular sample proportion is a little off from p or a lot off.

The formula can be built from properties of random variables you have already seen. Let X be the count of successes in n independent trials, each with probability of success p. X is a random variable, and its standard deviation, from the standard deviation rules for a count of independent successes, is the square root of n times p times (1 minus p). Since p-hat is just X divided by n, and dividing a random variable by a constant divides its standard deviation by that same constant, the standard deviation of p-hat equals the standard deviation of X divided by n: the square root of np(1-p), divided by n. Simplifying that fraction under a single square root gives the standard formula: the standard deviation of p-hat equals the square root of p(1-p)/n.

Here is a worked example. Suppose 40 percent of all registered voters in a large city support a proposed measure, so p = 0.4, and a pollster samples n = 50 voters. The standard deviation of p-hat is the square root of (0.4)(0.6)/50, which is the square root of 0.24/50, which is the square root of 0.0048, which is approximately 0.069. So sample proportions from repeated samples of 50 voters would typically differ from the true 0.4 by around 0.069, or about 6.9 percentage points.

Notice what the formula says about sample size: n sits in the denominator inside the square root, so larger samples produce a smaller standard deviation and therefore more precise estimates. This matches intuition, a poll of 50 people is noisier than a poll of 5000 people. It is also worth flagging a subtlety using the marble example from two chapters ago: there, p = 0.4 and n = 2, and the formula would predict a standard deviation of the square root of (0.4)(0.6)/2, which is the square root of 0.12, approximately 0.346. But the exact enumeration in that example gives a true standard deviation of 0.3, computed directly from the ten possible samples. The formula's answer, 0.346, does not match the exact answer, 0.3. That mismatch is not an error, it is a warning sign, and understanding why it happens is exactly the subject of the next chapter.
